title: Job 3:1–10
context: The narrator introduces the speech (3:1–2): after seven days and nights of silence with his three friends (2:11–13), Job opens his mouth and curses the day of his birth. From 3:3 the speaker is Job, and the chapter shifts from prose into poetry. In 3:3–10 Job asks that the day he was born and the night he was conceived be undone: darkened, left unsought by God, shut out of the calendar, and cursed by those who curse the day. He curses his day, not God: he does not renounce God, as Satan predicted (1:11; 2:5) and his wife urged (2:9). WEB’s wording is “Satan,” as in chapters 1–2, where whether the term is a title or a name is left open. Jeremiah 20:14–18 offers a close lament parallel by reference. The meaning of “those who rouse up leviathan” (3:8) is uncertain; many readers take leviathan here as a sea creature or chaos figure known from poetry (compare 41:1; Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1), and some suggest links to wider ancient Near Eastern imagery, though the precise background is debated. Both Arminian and Reformed readers treat the curse as honest lament spoken to and before God, neither a model of despair nor a sin to be corrected here; the book lets its later speeches and the LORD’s verdict on the friends (42:7) weigh Job’s words.

verses.text: After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed the day of his birth.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator frames the chapter: Job opens his mouth after long silence and curses the day of his birth, not God. Arminian readers note that Satan’s prediction (1:11; 2:5) fails even here, and that God’s relationship with Job leaves room for raw, honest speech that he will later answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that Job curses his day, not his God, and see the faith preserved through the prologue (1:22; 2:10) still holding beneath this grief. Shared ground: both traditions read the curse as lament within faith, not as apostasy, and let the book’s later verdict weigh it.

verses.arminianNotes: This brief formula marks the start of the poetic dialogue and the shift from narrative to speech. Arminian readers often observe that Job “answered” though no one has yet spoken to him, as if he is responding to his whole situation and, ultimately, to God, whose presence he never denies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see Job speaking into the silence of 2:13 and before God who has governed the events of chapters 1–2. Shared ground: both traditions take the narrator’s introduction as a cue that what follows is Job’s own voice, to be heard honestly and not yet weighed as the book’s conclusion.

verses.text: “Let the day perish in which I was born, the night which said, ‘There is a boy conceived.’
verses.arminianNotes: Job wishes the day of his birth and the night of his conception had perished, much as Jeremiah does in Jeremiah 20:14–18. Arminian readers hear the depth of real anguish in a man God genuinely values, and note that Scripture gives such words a place in prayer rather than silencing them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job’s birth and conception lay under God’s providence (compare Psalm 139:13–16), so Job’s curse is the cry of a sufferer who cannot see that purpose, not a denial of it. Shared ground: both traditions read this as poetic lament, not a literal request to alter the past or a verdict on the worth of life.

verses.text: Let that day be darkness. Don’t let God from above seek for it, neither let the light shine on it.
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks that his birthday become darkness and that God from above not seek it, a reversal of the creation call for light (Genesis 1:3). Arminian readers see Job speaking freely about God without cursing him, and stress that his relationship with God is strained but not broken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hear an undoing of creation language, with Job asking the Creator to forget one day of his ordering. They stress that God’s rule over days and nights is not overturned by the cry. Shared ground: both traditions take the imagery as lament, not a theory of how God governs time.

verses.text: Let darkness and the shadow of death claim it for their own. Let a cloud dwell on it. Let all that makes the day black terrify it.
verses.arminianNotes: Job piles up images of darkness, the shadow of death, cloud, and blackness to claim the day. Arminian readers hear the intensity of grief that can no longer find light, and note that the God who later answers Job (38:1) does not punish him for speaking his darkness aloud.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same imagery as the speech of a believer whose sight is clouded, while God’s care continues unseen (compare Psalm 139:11–12, where darkness is not dark to him). Shared ground: both traditions hold that God hears lament like this and that the book does not treat it as unbelief.

verses.text: As for that night, let thick darkness seize on it. Let it not rejoice among the days of the year. Let it not come into the number of the months.
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks that the night of his conception be seized by thick darkness and dropped from the calendar. Arminian readers see a man wishing his own story had never begun, and they stress that God’s patience with such words reflects his genuine, relational care for suffering people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the calendar Job wants to erase belongs to God, who numbers days and months (compare 14:5). The wish is grief, not rebellion. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetic intensity, and both decline to treat Job as already condemned for speaking this way.

verses.text: Behold, let that night be barren. Let no joyful voice come therein.
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks that his night be barren, with no joyful voice in it, inverting the joy that usually greets a birth. Arminian readers hear how loss has drained Job’s memory of gladness, and note that God’s later response engages Job rather than dismissing his pain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same inversion and see a sufferer who, for now, cannot trace God’s kindness in his own beginning. They hold that the kindness remained real. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as lament that Scripture records honestly, without endorsing despair as the truth about Job’s life.

verses.text: Let them curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up leviathan.
verses.arminianNotes: Job calls on those who curse the day and are ready to rouse up leviathan. Many readers take leviathan as a sea creature or chaos figure (compare 41:1; Psalm 74:14), and some suggest ancient Near Eastern background, though this is uncertain. Arminian readers stress that Job reaches for the strongest curse he can imagine, without cursing God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD later describes leviathan as his own creature, beyond human control (41:1–11), which places even this dark image under God’s rule. Who the cursers are is debated. Shared ground: both traditions hedge the background and read the line as Job’s heightened lament, not as approval of occult practice.

verses.text: Let the stars of its twilight be dark. Let it look for light, but have none, neither let it see the eyelids of the morning,
verses.arminianNotes: Job wants his night to wait for light that never comes, never seeing the eyelids of the morning. Arminian readers note the irony that Job, who longs for this night to stay dark, will himself wait long for light, and that God does finally speak to him out of the storm (38:1).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the longing for unending night as the speech of a man who cannot yet see the dawn God is preparing (compare 42:10–17). They do not take it as Job’s settled view of God. Shared ground: both traditions hold that the image expresses anguish and that the book’s later chapters answer it.

verses.text: because it didn’t shut up the doors of my mother’s womb, nor did it hide trouble from my eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: Job names the reason for his curse: that night did not shut the doors of the womb or hide trouble from his eyes. Arminian readers hear the core of his grief in his suffering, not in rejection of God, and note that he still speaks as one who expects his life to have meaning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job assumes his birth and his trouble fall within the order of things God governs, even while he cannot understand why (compare 10:8–12). Shared ground: both traditions see the verse as the hinge of the curse, rooted in pain rather than unbelief, and neither treats it as a sin to be corrected here.
